extracted.intended_audience: students, instructors, and administrators interested in university natural history education and practicing naturalists
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and curricular requirements for natural history instruction at Harvard University (college and scientific school), covering pedagogy, required courses/electives, laboratory and field training, assessment (note-books/exams), honours/thesis requirements, and higher-degree (D.Sc.) preparation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational second-year science courses (12 hours/week)
rubrics_metrics.description: At the commencement of his second year he may begin his studies by courses which lay the foundations of a knowledge of chemistry, geography, geology, and meteorology, taught by text-books, lectures, and excursions in the field. The time allowed for these studies during the year is estimated at twelve hours per week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is expected that the student will in this year lay the foundations for the work he may wish to do during the following years, by getting that general idea of the physics of the globe which forms the necessary basis for the work of the naturalist in any department of labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigator-first pedagogy: work upon natural objects
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle on which the teaching of zoology is based is that the student should at the very beginning be put into the position of an investigator. The student is at first required to do all his work upon natural objects, beginning with simple specimens (e.g. a Fungia), being required to draw and describe the specimen, aided only by such questions and suggestions as may be necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Progressive, hands-on sequence: start with simple object, then compare with other specimens (e.g. Manacena or Agaricea), make diagrammatic drawings from a dozen other specimens, use lectures to supplement direct observation. Individual teaching is given without weakening self-reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of diagrams in early study
rubrics_metrics.description: Care is taken to avoid the use of diagrams; this avoidance being dictated by the conviction that the student remembers the diagram and not the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises direct observation and memory of real specimens rather than reliance on schematic representations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Junior/second-year advanced courses and historical study
rubrics_metrics.description: Second-year courses include advanced zoology, palaeontology, historical geology, geography, and advanced botany; three lectures or readings per week discuss the history of zoology and palaeontology with special reference to modern opinions concerning the relations of animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students are given opportunities to consult major works and to learn methods of the masters; palaeontology students are required to traverse the relevant portions of Dana's Manual to learn characteristic fossils practically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Half-year advanced microscopy practical (4 hours/week)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the choice of subject the largest liberty is allowed, but the student is recommended during a half-year to study advanced microscopy; in this work the aid of an instructor is given for four hours a week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In four months the student should acquire sufficient knowledge of the practical management of the instrument in all ordinary investigations; the laboratory is well supplied with instruments for instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping full and accurate note-books as assessment criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest value in this work is set upon the keeping of full and accurate note-books. The rank of the student turns upon the condition of his note-books as much as upon the quarterly examinations which he is required to pass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note-books serve both as a record of work and a measure of ability to observe and express findings; they are tied to rank and assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for honours in zoology/palaeontology
rubrics_metrics.description: Those students who desire to contend for honours at the graduation in zoology or in palaeontology are required to have taken, besides their junior election in natural history, one election in physical science, and at least three natural history elections in the senior year, in all of which they must have attained excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are moreover required to write an acceptable thesis, which must contain an original discussion of some question in biological science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Junior electives and substitution of scientific theses
rubrics_metrics.description: Hereafter the junior electives will consist of a course in anatomy and physiology, one in zoology, and one in botany; and the students in this as well as in the last year will be allowed to substitute for the themes required in other branches theses upon scientific subjects prepared under the direction of their instructor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows substitution of research theses for standard themes, promoting original scientific work under instructor supervision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific School three-year B.Sc. course and admission
rubrics_metrics.description: A three years' course has been arranged which secures to the student a broad view over the whole field of science and the advantage which comes from a knowledge of the methods of research in use in its several branches. Students who can pass the required examinations are admitted to the degree of bachelor of science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graduates of colleges where science is effectively taught may enter in advanced standing; college graduates with honours in natural history may obtain this degree in one year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training in clear expression and preparation of theses
rubrics_metrics.description: The student is trained in the important art of expressing himself clearly on the matters which he is studying, by requiring him to keep carefully planned note-books; and he is urged to the preparation of theses which may embody the results of some research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ample opportunities provided for field studies by excursions during term and vacation led by instructors in zoology, botany, and geology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctor of Science (D.Sc.) candidacy and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: After two years' further study, one of which must be spent in Cambridge, the student may apply for the degree of doctor of science, which is given after an examination conducted by a committee appointed by the Academic Council of the University.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparation must be in some special department; the student will generally become the private pupil of some professor. The degree is a certificate of capacity as an investigator or teacher in the chosen science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Palaeontology practical requirement (Dana's Manual)
rubrics_metrics.description: The student who takes the elective in palaeontology is required to traverse the ground covered in that part of 'Dana's Manual' which is entitled historical geology, acquainting himself in a practical way with the most important characteristic fossils of the several periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises practical acquaintance with characteristic fossils as part of palaeontological training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laboratory/instrument provision and instructional staffing
rubrics_metrics.description: The scientific departments have a list of twenty-four instructors, and the material resources ... have cost in the aggregate over a million and a half of dollars. There are six museums in the University ... these collections ... furnish an efficient basis for the acquisition of the wide ranging knowledge on which a scientific career must be based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opportunities for contact and intercourse in scientific societies are excellent; there is a working society of natural history in the University and access to the Boston Society of Natural History.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental condition: ice must be at the melting point for regelation experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: In all the experiments referred to, ice at the melting point was used; when a block was cooled about a degree below the freezing-point, a shilling placed on it with pressure did not enter the ice, but after removing the freezing mixture (restoring melting-point conditions) the shilling passed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows that regelation (passage of bodies such as coins through ice) depends on the ice being at or very near the melting point; even a small decrease in temperature (~1°C) greatly increases resistance to the process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of thermal conductivity of the object in regelation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the coins had been non-conductors of heat, they would not have passed through the ice. Test: shilling with india-rubber disc (non-conductor) between shillings sank only about an eighth of an inch under similar load.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates that heat transfer through a conducting object (metal coin) is essential to the melting-regelation mechanism observed; non-conductors inhibit the required heat exchange.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure-temperature interplay and limits of glacier analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: The freezing point of water is lowered by pressure; but the lowering is very small (e.g. 163 atmospheres lowers freezing point by 0.13°C), so the very small differences in temperature combined with poor conductivity of ice and rock make the experiments not directly analogous to glacier motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For glaciers, heat conduction distances and poor conductivities mean exchange of heat is much slower; where ice is below freezing by even one degree, enormous resistance exists and regelation-like passage is unlikely to operate as in small-scale coin experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Yellowstone springs by dominant deposit: calcareous (lime) vs siliceous (silica)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two classes of springs in the Yellowstone valley, one in which lime predominates, in the other silica.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calcareous springs (e.g. White Mountain) form terraces of carbonate of lime; siliceous springs (most in Yellowstone/Firehole basins) form deposits of silica and display varied colours and textures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivision of siliceous springs by activity and temperature
rubrics_metrics.description: Siliceous springs may be divided into intermittent, boiling and spouting, and quiet springs. Those of the first class are always above boiling point during the period of action, but during the interval the temperature lowers to 150°. Those of the second are always at the boiling point, and some throw water by regular pulsations. The third may have been geysers but are now quiet and have a wide range of temperature from 188° to 80°.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temperature ranges and activity determine deposit chemistry (e.g. sesquioxide of iron deposits when temperature is reduced below 150°) and morphological behaviour (mud springs, steam jets, terraces).
